title: Pleasing God · Chapter 8: Those Who Do Not Please God
speaker: Joshua Heward-Mills
text:
Chapter 8

# Those Who Do Not Please God

Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea; And did all eat the same spiritual meat; And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ. But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted. Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand. Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents. Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer. Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come. Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.

1 Corinthians 10:1-12 (KJV)

This portion of Scripture starts with a warning. Paul is writing to Christians, and he's warning every Christian not to be unaware or ignorant of this story. Of all the Bible stories, the Holy Spirit is intent that every Christian should know this story. These things were our examples. The story of Israel coming out of Egypt was actually written for you—for your example and your advice.

Think about the people being described. They were under the cloud. They passed through the sea. They were baptised unto Moses. They ate spiritual meat and drank spiritual drink. The rock from which they drank was Christ. Yet with many of them God was not well pleased.

Remember, these people are not unbelievers. He's not talking about drunkards or idol worshippers. He's talking about the chosen people of God. Before we look at why they did not please God, let's look at their credentials. What were they doing right?

Before we examine what was wrong, consider their credentials.

# a. They lived under the manifest presence of God.

And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night: He took not away the pillar of the cloud by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from before the people.

Exodus 13:21-22 (KJV)

The Lord Himself went before them. The cloud was not merely an interesting natural phenomenon. They lived under His guidance and presence.

In the same way, a Christian may know what it is to sense the presence of God. There can be a stillness that makes a person weep, an atmosphere in which the heart is deeply moved, or an awareness of God so strong that one hardly wants to move.

The fact that you've enjoyed the manifest presence of God, that stillness where your hair stands up, where the atmosphere is so strong you don't even want to open your eyes—that doesn't mean you're living a life that pleases God. They were under the cloud. But it wasn't their cloud. They were enjoying the presence of God that was following Moses.

The people were enjoying the cloud that led them with Moses. The presence in the gathering could not take the place of their own obedience.

# b. They experienced miracles and deliverance.

They passed through the sea. They saw a way open where there had been no way and saw the pursuing Egyptians overwhelmed. They had been delivered from the captivity of Egypt.

Egypt gives us a picture of the world from which God saves us. A person may have come out of the world into church, seen miracles, experienced a breakthrough, or received a remarkable answer. These are good things. But they do not, by themselves, answer every question about whether God is pleased with that person's present life.

# c. They were committed followers of Moses.

This might be called their “baptism”—baptized both in sea and cloud!—as followers of Moses—their commitment to him as their leader.

1 Corinthians 10:2 (TLB)

Their baptism unto Moses speaks of identification with him and commitment to him as their leader. These were not people without a teacher. They were led by one of God's great servants.

You too may be in a good church, know the pastor personally, follow the teaching, read the books, and receive help from a sound ministry. Being close to the pastor is not a substitute for having a heart that pleases God.

# d. They ate spiritual food.

They did not lack what God supplied. In our lives, hearing powerful messages and receiving good teaching are privileges. We can attend the series, the camps, and the Bible studies and still need to ask what is happening within us.

# e. They drank spiritual drink.

They received from the rock, and that rock was Christ. You may have tasted the anointing and known the Spirit's ministry. Yet the passage immediately says that God was not well pleased with many of these people.

These are saved, cloud-covered, well-fed, so-called spiritual people of God, led by one of God's greatest servants, Moses. Yet they didn't live lives that pleased God. Your powerful encounters with God and the Bible-based church you attend, although very good things, don't necessarily mean God is pleased with your life. There were other things they allowed to pollute their hearts and lives.

So be careful. If you are thinking, “Oh, I would never behave like that”—let this be a warning to you. For you too may fall into sin.

1 Corinthians 10:12 (TLB)

The warning at the end is especially important: if you think you stand, take heed lest you fall. Do not read the passage with the comfortable thought that you could never be like them. Let it examine you.

# 1. God is not pleased with those who lust after evil things.

It's not what you are doing. It's not what you have. What you desire makes you somebody who irritates God. Even though Israel had come out of Egypt, they maintained their lust and desire for the world. They had come out of Egypt, but they left their hearts there.

Israel had left Egypt, but something of Egypt remained attractive within them. They had come out physically while their affections looked backwards.

And the mixt multitude that was among them fell a lusting: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat? We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick: But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.

Numbers 11:4-6 (KJV)

They remembered the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. They had God's provision before them, but their hearts were occupied with what they missed. They spoke of the manna as though it were nothing.

We all think God was upset about complaining. But God was upset about lust. The murmuring irritated Him, but the lust—the fact that you want something else. It's not about what you're eating. It's about what you're lusting for. It's not about what you have. It's about what your heart is desiring.

You can be saved and still desire the world. You can be in church while money, a particular relationship, an admired lifestyle, or some personal ambition is what fills your heart.

Ask not merely, “What am I doing?” but, “What do I want?” A pastor needs to ask that question too. Being involved in spiritual work does not exempt the desire from God's assessment.

Moses presents a different heart. His concern was to have God Himself.

Now therefore, I pray thee, if I have found grace in thy sight, shew me now thy way, that I may know thee, that I may find grace in thy sight: and consider that this nation is thy people. And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest. And he said unto him, If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence.

Exodus 33:13-15 (KJV)

He did not want a promised destination without God's presence. The place could not replace the Person.

When we considered Abraham, we saw a test concerning the son he loved and the God who had given him. I have come to see how widely that question applies: is God Himself enough for us? We can want what He gives while being unwilling to choose Him above the gift.

Even in the sufferings of Jesus, the cry of forsakenness shows us the weight of His fellowship with the Father.

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?

Matthew 27:46 (KJV)

What do you want from God? What if the thing you are pursuing became a rival to Him in your heart? Why should He place something close to you that will become the very thing drawing you away?

Somebody came to see me and said that I looked stressed and tired, and offered to arrange a massage. In reassuring my wife, the person was saying that this woman would not be competition. It made me think: why should God let money come close to you when money is His competition? Why should He supply you with the very idol that will take you away from Him?

Why do we want Him to supply an idol? Why do we insist that a particular thing must be added before we can be satisfied with Him?

God has tested me with money. I've walked away from money so many times—salaries, payments, luxury living. I've walked away from many things, and I'm still being tested all the time. What's in your heart? What's inside? What do you want?

The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.

Jeremiah 17:9-10 (KJV)

Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.

Psalm 139:23-24 (KJV)

The heart is deceitful. Who can know it? We all think we know our hearts. Who can know it? That's why David says, “Search me, O Lord. See if there's any wicked way.”

The point is not simply the nationality, appearance, or possessions of the person you marry. The question is whether you are demanding your own preference or sincerely wanting God's will. I do not want a particular category of person more than I want what He has for me.

The same applies to money, travel, music, and the world we left behind. You can be outwardly walking with God while inwardly wishing you were somewhere else.

Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:

Colossians 3:5 (KJV)

Covetousness is called idolatry. Strong desire is not spiritually neutral merely because it has not yet become a visible act.

As I've been married and pastored marriages, I've come to appreciate things about my wife that I didn't used to value. My wife wants nothing from me. What she wanted when she married was to marry me. I used to find it irritating. “If there's something, ask me.” But now I understand. Some people wanted more than you. If you cut everything else out and say, “It's just me,” they don't want it. They want what you come with, or what they thought you were coming with.

I've come to understand God when He says, “Want only Me. Your heart—want only Me.”

We must not speak of salvation, His presence, and His daily provision as though they mean nothing because we have not yet received a husband, a job, a car, or another thing on our list. The manna was God's gift. Their contempt for it exposed their desire for Egypt.

To whom our fathers would not obey, but thrust him from them, and in their hearts turned back again into Egypt,

Acts 7:39 (KJV)

They didn't go back to Egypt, but in their hearts they turned back to Egypt. It's descriptive of Christians today: come out of the world, but in our hearts we're still in the world.

Desire is also where sin begins to gain a foothold.

But each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust. Then when lust has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin is accomplished, it brings forth death.

James 1:14-15 (NASB 1995)

The picture is of conception, birth, and a final result. Deal with the beginning rather than waiting until the whole outcome has arrived.

“I must have this. I must have this job. I must have this money. I must have these people's approval. I must wear these clothes.” It's your lust for money that made you a thief. The desire to be accepted, loved, special to somebody—it's burning in you. When lust conceives, it's just a matter of time before it gives birth to sin.

Do not continually feed the desire and then act surprised when it produces sin. Cut it off at its root.

Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.

Proverbs 6:25 (KJV)

The way you look can nourish a desire. Do not cultivate an attraction that will pull you away from what is right. Give attention instead to the person and commitments God has already placed in your life.

We can be under the cloud, hearing from Moses, eating spiritual food, and still carrying a desire that displeases God. Let Him deal with what you want.

# 2. God is not pleased with those who have idols.

Israel's idolatry exposes impatience, ingratitude, and a lack of devotion. As long as Moses was present, they followed. When he was away, they demanded something else to lead them.

Saying unto Aaron, Make us gods to go before us: for as for this Moses, which brought us out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him. And they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice unto the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands.

Acts 7:40-41 (KJV)

They made a calf, offered sacrifices to it, and rejoiced in the work of their hands. Two things stand out: sacrifice and rejoicing.

Your idol is who you sacrifice to and who you rejoice in. They offered sacrifice to the idol, and they rejoiced. The thing you sacrifice your time, money, effort, family, and heart for—that is your god. What makes you happy? The thing that, when you don't have it, makes you sad. What you rejoice in—that's your idol.

She's your idol. He's your idol. The car is your idol. The job is your idol. Clothes, hair, friends, shoes, a visa, a green card, travelling. What are you pursuing? What are you chasing? What are you looking forward to, thinking that when you get it, everything will be all right?

The account also describes the people sitting down to eat and drink and rising up to play. The activity was not an innocent replacement for worship.

And they rose up early on the morrow, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.

Exodus 32:6 (KJV)

And when Moses saw that the people were naked; (for Aaron had made them naked unto their shame among their enemies:)

Exodus 32:25 (KJV)

The Living Bible says:

nor worship idols as they did. (The Scriptures tell us, “The people sat down to eat and drink and then got up to dance” in worship of the golden calf.)

1 Corinthians 10:7 (TLB)

The Amplified Bible brings out the immoral activities:

Do not be worshipers of handmade gods, as some of them were; just as it is written [in Scripture], “ The people sat down to eat and drink [after sacrificing to the golden calf at Horeb], and stood up to play [indulging in immoral activities].”

1 Corinthians 10:7 (AMP)

The New International Version describes revelry:

Do not be idolaters, as some of them were; as it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry.”

1 Corinthians 10:7 (NIV)

The Amplified Bible, Classic Edition, says:

Do not be worshipers of false gods as some of them were, as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink [the sacrifices offered to the golden calf at Horeb] and rose to sport (to dance and give way to jesting and hilarity).

1 Corinthians 10:7 (AMPC)

The Good News Translation puts it plainly:

nor to worship idols, as some of them did. As the scripture says, “The people sat down to a feast which turned into an orgy of drinking and sex.”

1 Corinthians 10:7 (GNT)

Idolatry and immoral conduct can become closely connected. A person may appear to be pursuing sexual pleasure when the deeper idol is money, acceptance, or the lifestyle the arrangement supplies.

Do not deal only with the visible behaviour while protecting the thing being worshipped underneath it. Ask God to show you what you sacrifice for and what you rejoice in.

# 3. God is not pleased with those who commit fornication.

The instruction in 1 Corinthians 10 is direct: we are not to commit fornication as some of them did. There is no need to search for a special revelation to make the warning clear.

For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;

1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 (KJV)

This is the will of God. Church attendance, tithing, gifts, spiritual experiences, and closeness to a pastor cannot turn sexual sin into something acceptable to Him.

Be honest about what is happening. Stop hiding behind the version of your life that everybody can see in church. Confess the sin, seek the help you need, and turn from it. Knowing the right people and receiving good teaching do not remove the responsibility to obey.

The passage records a terrible fall in a single day. Let the warning reach us before we imagine that spiritual privileges put us beyond consequences.

# 4. God is not pleased with those who tempt Christ.

To tempt God is to test Him, like the people of Israel did. They didn't believe God had the power to take care of them in the wilderness. To them, the circumstances and surroundings meant that it was impossible to survive and thrive. “Let's see if God is good. I'm not sure. I don't believe God can take care of me.”

There is a difference between trusting His promise and demanding that He repeatedly prove Himself before we will obey.

And they sinned yet more against him by provoking the most High in the wilderness. And they tempted God in their heart by asking meat for their lust. Yea, they spake against God; they said, Can God furnish a table in the wilderness? Behold, he smote the rock, that the waters gushed out, and the streams overflowed; can he give bread also? can he provide flesh for his people? Therefore the LORD heard this, and was wroth: so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and anger also came up against Israel; Because they believed not in God, and trusted not in his salvation:

Psalm 78:17-22 (KJV)

“Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?” That's how we tempt and test God. “Can He do it? God has to prove Himself before I take a step. Let me see certain signs before I commit.” That's a test of God. He doesn't like it. He struck the rock, and the waters gushed out. Then they said, “But can He give bread?” That's how we are with God.

We can do the same. We know that He has saved us, but then wonder whether He can care for our future, provide what we need, or lead us into the right marriage. We make the next step of obedience conditional on another demonstration.

God wants us to trust His Word. He has not become unable to provide because the scenery around us has changed.

Because all those men which have seen my glory, and my miracles, which I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tempted me now these ten times, and have not hearkened to my voice;

Numbers 14:22 (KJV)

He counted the times they had tempted Him. They had seen His glory and miracles and still would not hearken to His voice.

You've seen My glory. You've seen My miracles. You've seen what I did in Egypt, and you're still testing Me these ten times. Has God not looked after you? If there's a change in your circumstances, you're questioning God again: “Will it be okay? Will it be all right?” He's done a lot. The least He deserves from me is trust.

A person once asked me to help pass on a gift that God had prompted for another pastor. It was a beautiful response of obedience. We should learn to respond to His leading rather than continually placing His ability in a test tube.

Do what He says and trust Him to care for you. He deserves more than a succession of demands that He prove He can do it again.

# 5. God is not pleased with those who murmur and complain.

And don’t murmur against God and his dealings with you as some of them did, for that is why God sent his Angel to destroy them.

1 Corinthians 10:10 (TLB)

Do not murmur against God and His dealings with you. The passage warns that some of Israel's people were destroyed in connection with this very thing.

Paul speaks of a different attitude.

Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.

Philippians 4:11-12 (KJV)

This is not a theory. This is not just a teaching. You've got to learn to be content. I know what it's like not to have what I need. I also know what it's like to have more than I need. I've learned the secret of being content. No matter what happens, I'm content—well fed or hungry, more than enough or not enough.

But godliness with contentment is great gain.

1 Timothy 6:6 (KJV)

We've got a lot of godly people who are not content. You're godly, but you're not happy with your wife. Godly, but you don't like the area you live in. Godly, but you're not happy with how the church is being led. Add to your godliness contentment.

We must learn to live with human limitations. Not everything and everybody can be remade into the exact shape we prefer.

Consider the work of God: for who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked?

Ecclesiastes 7:13 (KJV)

Consider the work of God. We are often trying to force everything into a perfectly straight line. Even the shapes of the natural world should make us think about how little of life fits the rigid pattern we demand.

This reaches into marriage. A quiet person does not become an outgoing person merely because a spouse insists. A familiar weakness may not be a personal insult aimed at you. It may be something the person has struggled with for a long time.

A husband once came to discuss several frustrations with his wife. As he described them, I recognised traits I already knew. They were not new behaviours invented against him. Understanding that did not make every weakness ideal, but it helped locate the problem more honestly.

Do not envy another person's spouse merely because you see an attractive public picture. You do not know the whole of the private life. Comparison is a poor foundation for contentment.

The same applies to a church. I have made appointments I should not have made. Sometimes discipline has been too severe; sometimes it has been too soft. There have been failures, gaps, and decisions that could have been better. I do not claim perfection.

But the people assessing a church are not perfect either. Somebody may neglect prayer and the Word, yet be consumed with criticising the arrangement of the chairs. We can become demanding about other people's responsibilities while giving ourselves great allowance in our own lives.

I'm okay with the church members God has given me. I'm not looking for another church. I understand my office. If a pastor's couch could repeat what it has heard! But I've not said I don't like my members. I'm also not perfect. I don't purport to be perfect. I don't want to lead people who expect me to be perfect, because your expectations won't be met.

We must not confuse an endless complaint with the pursuit of righteousness. We should be humble enough to recognise the mercy we ourselves need while we are speaking about somebody else's imperfection.

There are things we dislike in a person that are also connected with qualities from which we benefit. The energy that feels noisy in one setting may be part of the life that person brings to the home. The strong voice that irritates us may also belong to somebody who works hard on the family's behalf.

A man’s belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; and with the increase of his lips shall he be filled.

Proverbs 18:20 (KJV)

I used to complain about the noise my wife and children made as they came towards the house. I could hear them laughing and talking before they reached the door. Yet when they were away for a week, I discovered a silence louder than the noise. The house was orderly, the food was there, and things were in place, but the people were missing.

When I came into the house, the silence was louder than the noise. Everything was arranged, everything was tidy, everything was straight. There was food, there was everything—but silence. My friends, be content with such things as you have.

Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.

Hebrews 13:5 (KJV)

He has said that He will not leave us or forsake us. Let that promise teach us contentment. Do not postpone all satisfaction until a person, a church, or a situation has become the perfect thing you imagined.

# Take the warning personally.

The people in this passage experienced the cloud, the sea, Moses' leadership, spiritual food, and spiritual drink. Yet many of them did not please God. Their story should reach beyond the page into our own hearts.

Examine desire, idolatry, sexual sin, the testing of God, and the spirit of complaint. Do not use a spiritual experience to avoid what Scripture is showing you.

These things were written for our admonition. They concern those upon whom the ends of the world have come. The story of the Exodus has something urgent to say to believers now.

Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.

1 Corinthians 10:11 (KJV)

So be careful. If you are thinking, “Oh, I would never behave like that”—let this be a warning to you. For you too may fall into sin.

1 Corinthians 10:12 (TLB)

Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. Do not assume that the warning is only for somebody else. Let us live to please Him.
